newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cargo thefts funding in doubt.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cargo thefts funding in doubt.

text.p: Shippers, alarmed about the increasing problem with cargo theft, are concerned that $1.1 million of Congressional funding to battle the problem in South Florida has not yet made it to the law enforcement task force on the front line.
"The task force will die without funding," said Alfred T. Checkett, head of corporate security for Calvin Klein Cosmetics Co., New York.

On October 1, police put more muscle into the assault on cargo crime in South Florida with the formation of a task force that included 14 full time officers from the Metro-Dade Police Department, Federal Bureau of Investigation, and Florida Department of Law Enforcement. The U.S. Customs Department is also involved.

The $1.1 million, Checkett said, was to be used for "buy" money, equipment and other costs of front-line police work. But, he said the Justice Department plans to use the money for prosecutors salaries.
The U.S. Justice department spokesman John Russell said only: "We will attempt to utilise available resources to fight cargo theft including support of local investigators of the task force."
Florida Senator Connie Mack, who was instrumental in getting the funding for South Florida, declined to discuss the funding question.

But spokesman for Connie Mack, Jeff Cohen said "We will closely monitor the situation and see how the Justice Department uses these resources. We will make sure Florida businesses and citizens are protected from the scourge of cargo theft."

Cargo theft is estimated to be a $10 billion problem with most of the merchandise stolen in Miami, New York/New Jersey and Los Angeles, said Edward Badolato, head of the National Cargo Security Council, a trade group of shippers and transportation executives.
"We are obviously very concerned about cargo theft and we want this program to move forward," said Badolato.
Cargo theft is becoming more violent with truck drivers and warehouse employees being assaulted.
"It is a new breed of crooks. They are shifting from drugs to cargo theft," said Badalato. Cargo theft is just as lucrative as drugs and the penalties are lighter, said Badolato.

For now, the task force is making do with rental cars and borrowed cameras. Lt. Edward Peto, head of the task force, said the $1.1 million would make catching the crooks a lot easier. His wish list: overtime pay, vehicles and video and camera equipment.

For their part, some crime-weary air cargo shippers threaten to take their business out of Miami to other ports, which are eager for their business. Says Checkett: "If you are at risk when you walk down the street, you change the street you walk down." -Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
